BREAKING: US diesel inventories dropped -3.6 million barrels last week, to 99.3 million barrels, the lowest level since May 2003.

Since January 2026, distillate fuel oil inventories have declined -33.7 million barrels, or -25%.

Furthermore, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell -399,000 barrels last week, to 282.2 million barrels, its lowest since October 1982.

Since March, oil inventories in the SPR have dropped by -133.2 million barrels, or -32%.

Meanwhile, commercial crude oil stocks excluding the SPR declined -865,000 barrels last week, to 409.8 million barrels, their lowest reading since July 31st.

US fuel reserves are being depleted at a rapid pace.

When existential systems are updated, it requires extreme vetting. Old tech is sometimes good, actually, if it's isolated and maintained as critical. https://t.co/nOt1Ni8gNH

Source: I worked for 12 years at the FAA in their simulation division for new technology.

The FAA isn't perfect, but much like the nuclear arsenal and major bank backups, you absolutely want to minimize overhauling the core system until you absolutely have to.

As funny as this headline is, there's a reason for it.

They kept the nuclear systems on this tech until like 2019. The FAA is phasing out now.

Super-secure slow-update tech like nuclear, air traffic, or banking, doesn't want to touch the outside world for as long as possible.

Seeing a lot of tweets about blown up hedge funds. It certainly makes sense. A lot of funds run with too much leverage. In addition, they often allow monthly or quarterly redemptions which inconveniently means they get redemption requests at exactly the wrong times. To make matters worse, if they have a whole team of traders and analysts, these folks often abandon ship as soon as they realize they won’t see a bonus for some time because the fund is too far below its high watermark.

Personally, I was never interested in this model. To invest in a concentrated way in highly volatile small cap equities, I believe you need permanent or quasi-permanent capital. I also don’t think you can build up a huge cost structure that needs to be fed.

I started my fund with only 1 super long term oriented outside investor. I said no to every other request to invest. I was wealthy before I started and there are no employees to feed. Nobody is calling me. Nobody wants to redeem. As I’ve said for years, I use derivatives on a very limited basis (1-2% of capital) and use very light margin most of the time.

So, as much as my haters will be annoyed to hear this, I am not going anywhere. I will be here, weathering the storm, staying invested, helping my companies.

This is what long term builders do.

On today's stock market crash:

As an investor, on days like today, you have to ask yourself one question: What fundamentally changed over the last 24 hours?

The shift in the fundamental backdrop cannot be attributed solely to the Midterm Election results; markets had already largely priced in the outcome.

So, what changed between yesterday and today? What is the fundamental reason for today's decline?

One of the most likely catalysts is growing concern about a potential "ban" on AI, or at the very least, severe regulation of the industry.

Over the last 24 hours, Democratic lawmakers have publicly called for restrictions on advanced AI development, including an outright "ban on artificial superintelligence."

Frankly, an outright ban will not happen.

Such a ban, if even possible to enforce, would effectively mean the US surrendering its position in the global AI race to China.

Does this mean AI is "over" or today's stock market crash marks "the end?" Absolutely not.

Rather, we believe we are witnessing a sudden shift in sentiment colliding with excessive levels of leverage, potentially triggering forced liquidations by several major institutional investors.

Therefore, today's downturn is more technical than fundamental. This is not to discount the concerns around regulation, they are legitimate. But price action right now does not look orderly or rational.

We are in the midst of the biggest technological revolution in human history.

Zoom out and remain calm.

Speaking of the dot com bust… We all know the caveat that price analogs are silly and for entertainment purposes only. Yet, the analog between the AI melt-up since April 2025 and the dot com bubble from October 1998 until March 2000 keeps rhyming with uncanny precision. It’s bound to break at some point, but for now both the time dimension and the price magnitude have been identical, just in time for the negative headlines to start around neocloud credit spreads and capex plans.
